newsitem.title: USA: Bank profits grew in third quarter, but credit woes persist.
newsitem.headline: Bank profits grew in third quarter, but credit woes persist.

text.p: Major U.S. banks, led by Chase Manhattan Corp. and Citicorp., Tuesday reported strong gains for the latest quarter, but amid continuing concern about consumer credit.

Chase, which overtook Citicorp this year as the nation's largest bank company after its merger with Chemical Banking Corp., said its earnings in the third quarter rose to $858 million, up 12 percent from $764 million in the same period of 1995.
Citicorp said it earned $935 million in the period, up 11 percent from $877 million a year ealier.
Nationsbank, the nation's fifth largest bank, said it earned $625 million, or $2.12 a share, up from $530 million, or $1.95 a share.

The results at Chase included after-tax merger-related expenses of $32 million, but merger savings in the quarter were $180 million. The company said it expected to achieve merger savings of $510 million in 1996.
Chase and Chemical merged on March 31. The year-ago comparisons were made as though the merger had been in effect for all periods.

"We continued to demonstrate revenue growth across both our global wholesale and nationwide consumer businesses," said Walter Shipley, chairman and chief executive officer. "We also stuck to the basics, effectively managing our operating and credit costs."
The corporation's return on average common stockholders' equity was 17.9 percent, which compared with 16.2 percent in the 1995 third quarter.
Credit card net charge-offs were $296 million, or 4.95 percent of average managed receivables. That compared with $279 million, or 4.78 percent, in the second quarter, Chase said.
Arthur Soter, analyst at Morgan Stanley & Co., said credit card lending was getting considerable attention because it was virtually the only problem area for the banks.
"Credit cards will continue to be an issue that investors in these banks will have to contend with for a while longer," Soter said.

He added that there was evidence the banks were slowing the growth of credit card portfolios, with solicitations down and standards raised. The tougher standards include shorter grace periods and higher late fees.
Chase said its earnings were equal to $1.80 a share, compared with $1.58 a share a year earlier.
Total assets as of Sept. 30 were $323 billion, compared with $308 billion a year earlier.
Chase also said it approved a common-stock repurchase programme for up to $2.5 billion of its common stock, which would total almost 7 percent of its outstanding shares.
Citicorp said income from its consumer operations fell to $466 million from $515 million, partly as a result of higher costs in its credit card business.
It said charge-offs due to non-payment on credit cards were at a rate of 5.11 percent of outstanding domestic credit card debt, up from 4.99 percent in the second quarter.
U.S. bankcard loans delinquent 90 days or more were 1.86 percent of the portfolio vs. 1.73 percent at the end of the second quarter and 1.54 percent a year ago, the company said.
Its worldwide card business earned $243 million in the quarter, down from $290 million a year ago.
Citicorp said net income from its corporate banking business worldwide was $520 million versus $389 million a year ago.
Citicorp's net earnings were equal to $1.85 a share, up from $1.79 a share a year earlier.
Citicorp's stock gained $1.375 to $94.75 on the New York Stock Exchange. Chase was unchanged at $82.50, also on the NYSE. Nationsbank, based in Charlotte, N.C., was down 50 cents at $88.75.

Among other banks, San Francisco based Wells Fargo earned $321 million, up from $261 million; Banc One Corp. in Columbus, Ohio, earned $355 million, up from $331 million; Bank of New York earned $249 million, up from $234 million; Chicago-based First Chicago NBD earned $358 million, up from $357 million; Mellon Bank, based in Pittsburgh, earned $172 million, up from $166 million.
